This course takes soil mid-infrared spectroscopy and rebuilds it inside R's [tidyverse](https://tidyverse.org/) and [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org). You'll load real spectrometer output and engineer features from it. Then you'll catch bad samples, fit and score a model, and run the same pipeline on a public global spectral library.

## Why tidyverse and tidymodels

Soil MIR spectroscopy already has capable, purpose-built R packages: `prospectr` and `resemble`, among others, cover preprocessing and spectral similarity in real depth. This course proposes an alternative: wrap that domain-specific work inside the tidyverse and tidymodels, the general frameworks most R users already know.

For me, four things make tidyverse and tidymodels worth building this course on. 

1. The abstractions read naturally. `recipe()`, `mutate()`, `step_snv()`, each one names what it does. That keeps your attention on the domain instead of on R itself while modelling. Knowing what's underneath still matters. This course spends real time unpacking it. But during modelling, the abstractions keep your attention on the pipeline rather than the implementation. 
2. tidymodels also provides a harness for modelling and validating rigorously: splitting, resampling, tuning, and evaluation all follow the same structure, one that's easy to get wrong by hand. A pipeline built this way is reproducible and repeatable. 
3. Build it once, reuse it again and again, on a new dataset, a new target, a colleague's laptop. 
4. And building on tidyverse and tidymodels means building on a vast, expressive, mainstream ecosystem, one this course borrows rather than reinvents.

Base `recipes` ships no steps for spectra. This course adds a handful, wrapping `prospectr` and `resemble` underneath. [Feature engineering](4-feature-engineering.qmd) tells that story properly. Everything downstream of them is standard tidymodels. We won't reteach the tidyverse's own documentation, its books, or its cheatsheets. Where this course points at a reference instead of re-explaining it, follow the link. That reference will outlast this course.

## How this course teaches

Each page runs top-down. It opens with the full step at the level you'd actually use day to day, one function call that returns a fitted model and a table of results. Only then does it open up to show what's inside. The course runs the same way: [The full pipeline](1-full-pipeline.qmd) assembles the whole thing once, then every page after it opens up one piece.

That's deliberate. R functions like `recipe()`, `mutate()`, and `tune()` name what they do closely enough that someone with limited R experience can run the pipeline and follow its logic, even before they could write any of it themselves. Only later does peeling back a layer become worth the time. Every page that unpacks a function names its source file. Digging further is always one open file and the R console away.

[R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) covers the R foundations this course assumes, or skips past to keep moving. The [Posit cheatsheets](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/) cover most packages this course uses, in a page or two each. If you want to understand R as a language, not just this pipeline, start with the Foundations section of [Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/). Finally, the [Tidy Modeling with R](https://www.tmwr.org/) book proposes a deep dive into the Tidymodels framework.

## The course

1. [Getting set up](0-getting-setup.qmd): install R, Positron, and the packages this course uses.
2. [The full pipeline](1-full-pipeline.qmd): load, preprocess, tune, test, and predict, once, end to end, before any of it gets explained.
3. [Loading spectral data](2-loading-data.qmd): read a folder of OPUS files and a wet chemistry CSV into one tibble.
4. [Exploratory data analysis](3-eda.qmd): look at the spectra and the soil properties before modelling anything.
5. [Feature engineering](4-feature-engineering.qmd): build a `recipes` pipeline out of resampling, SNV, and Savitzky-Golay steps.
6. [Outlier detection](5-outlier-detection.qmd): use PCA on the preprocessed spectra to find samples a model shouldn't trust.
7. [Evaluating performance](6-evaluating-performance.qmd): split the data, fit a model, and score it with tidymodels.
8. [Preparing a model for inference](7-preparing-for-inference.qmd): save a fitted model, load it again, and predict new spectra.
9. [Preparing OSSL](8-preparing-ossl.qmd): pull a working sample from the Open Soil Spectral Library.
10. [Predicting exchangeable potassium using OSSL](9-kex-ossl-pipeline.qmd): the same pipeline, run end to end on a public, global dataset.
